pages.text:
*From the Walk-Book of Highstep, Day 28. Weather: fair, and steaming. Distance: three miles. Direction: left. Population: three hundred and ninety-one. Goats: forty-one, including one from Lowbrook.*

The morning after the flood smelled of wet wool and warm goat, with clothes hanging on every rope bridge like a giant's laundry line. Lowbrook’s farm animals wandered through the pines, looking with the confused dignity of people who had just lost their map.

Mrs. Cobb, stout and straw-hatted, stood on a flat rock near Tor’s knee. She looked up, then down, before reaching out to pat the mossy flank of the mountain.

"That big lump," she announced to the crowd. "You're a bit damp today."

Highstep held its breath, waiting for a disaster that never came. Tor, who did not speak, gave a low, rumbling shiver that rolled through the soles of Mo’s bare feet. It was not a tremor of fear, but a deep, earthy chuckle that started in her belly and finished in her horns.

Mo grinned. Admiral the goat, who had followed them out of the river, bleated in agreement and tried to eat Mrs. Cobb’s shoe.
pages.image: A stout woman in a straw hat pats the mossy leg of a giant mountain-creature while a brown and white goat with a tin bell tries to eat her shoe, surrounded by drying laundry on ropes.

pages.text:
Mayor Marsh and Mrs. Cobb stood on a cheese crate, their voices rising in a chorus of logistics. They were two very large voices in small bodies, arguing over who controlled the salt supply.

"My people have been in one spot," said Marsh, adjusting her hat. "We know how to store things."

"My people have been in one spot," Mrs. Cobb countered, "and we know how to *eat* things. You can't ration a feeling."

It was a stalemate. Mo’s father, Tomás, looked at his mother. Mo’s mother, Marisol, looked at the crate. Then, with a sigh that emptied the air right out of the room, Mayor Marsh stepped down.

"Salt for the soup," she said. "And Mrs. Cobb, you tell the stories. We are all a bit thin on narrative."

Mrs. Cobb nodded, satisfied. That evening, the two villages shared a pot of broth that tasted of rain and hope. It turned out that Highstep and Lowbrook needed exactly the same things: salt, warmth, and a good story. The only difference was that Lowbrook had more salt, and Highstep had better puns.
pages.image: Two women, one in a tall hat and one in a straw hat, shake hands over a steaming wooden pot while villagers in ponchos and aprons gather around, looking hungry and happy.

pages.text:
Mo found Junie on the Footpost. She was sketching in her scrapbook, her yellow scarf tied tight, her curls damp from the river. She did not look up when he approached.

"I didn't know a mountain could be brave," she said, her voice quiet.

Mo sat down next to her, pressing one bare heel into the stone. "I didn't know I could be so bad at listening," he admitted.

They both started to apologize at the same time, then stopped, looking at each other. A laugh bubbled up, tired and relieved, like the sound of a kettle finally finishing its boil.

Junie turned the scrapbook toward him. On the page was a drawing of a still town, houses with square windows and no tilt. In the background, rising above the rooftops, stood a very large, shaggy mountain. It was not threatening. It was waiting.

"Is it... a home?" Mo asked.

"I'm not sure yet," Junie said, tapping her pencil against her lip. "But I think it's a start."
pages.image: A tall girl with dark curls and a yellow scarf shows a sketchbook to a boy in a green poncho, both sitting on a flat stone with a giant mossy mountain looming softly in the background.

pages.text:
Mo told her everything. He did not rush, as he had with the village, but he spoke slowly and in order. He paused when she asked questions and stopped when her brow furrowed in confusion. Then he handed her the torn page, the one Gran had hidden inside her walking staff for forty years.

Junie read it once. She read it again, her voice steady and clear. "When a mountain grows old, she walks to the sea... and lies down to rest."

She looked up at Mo, her eyes serious. "A house that stays still might not be the same as a home that stays still," she said, tapping her pencil against her lip. "I am not sure yet which one I want."

Mo nodded, feeling the heavy weight in his chest shift, not disappear, but lighten just enough to breathe.

"I am glad you told it properly," she said.

"Me too," Mo replied. "I think I forgot how to listen until I had to listen to you."

Junie smiled, a small, sharp expression that reached her eyes. "We are both learning," she said. "One day at a time. Or one step at a time, depending on who is walking."
pages.image: A boy hands a crumpled piece of paper to a girl on a stone platform; she reads it with wide eyes while a large goat chews on a nearby rope, the mood quiet and serious.

pages.text:
That night, the Green was full. Three hundred and ninety-one people crowded around a great communal fire, the light flickering on their faces. Gran stood on the cheese crate, her staff in one hand, the torn page in the other. She did not look old. She looked like the Stepkeeper she was.

She read the page in her clear, dry voice. Nobody laughed. The air was still, heavy with the scent of woodsmoke and pine. When she finished, the silence stretched, long and warm.

Then Mrs. Cobb cleared her throat. She was a woman who lived in one place all her life, a place with dirt roads and muddy boots. She looked up at Tor, who was resting her head low, her eyes half-closed, her hum a low vibration in the ground.

"Well," Mrs. Cobb said. "I've lived in one place all my life. I would like to see the sea."

The crowd murmured, a sound like wind through pines. Mo looked at Junie, who looked at the mountain. They were ready.
pages.image: An old woman with white hair and large spectacles holds up a paper to a crowd of people gathered around a fire, a giant mountain with kind eyes watching over them in the dark.
